definition: Computer software that does things we usually expect a human mind to do, like understanding language, spotting patterns or making decisions.
A way of building AI where the computer learns patterns from many examples instead of following rules a person wrote by hand.
AI that creates brand-new content, such as text, images, audio or video, instead of only sorting or labelling things that already exist.
An AI system trained on huge amounts of text so it can read and write human language. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are built on these.
The huge collection of text, images or other examples an AI learns from before you ever use it.
A program you talk to by typing or speaking; it replies in conversation. Modern ones are powered by large language models.
How a language model writes: it repeatedly guesses the most likely next word, so it sounds fluent without checking whether the facts are true.
The date after which an AI model has no training data, so it may not know about newer events unless it can search the web.
A small chunk of text, often a short word or part of a word, that an AI reads and writes one piece at a time.
The limit on how much text an AI can keep in view at once, covering your messages and its own replies in the current chat.
A feature that lets a chatbot save facts about you between chats, so you don't have to repeat them each time.
The instruction or question you type to an AI. The clearer and more complete it is, the better the answer you get.
A role you ask the AI to play, such as a friendly editor or a careful accountant, so it answers in the right style.
The attitude of a piece of writing, such as formal, friendly or firm. You can tell an AI which tone to use.
Asking an AI to do a task with instructions only and no examples of what a good answer looks like.
Showing an AI a few examples of what you want inside your prompt, so it copies the pattern in its answer.
The shape you want the answer in, such as a table, a bullet list, an email or numbered steps.
A rule you give an AI that limits its answer, such as a word limit or a list of things to avoid.
Improving an answer through several rounds of follow-up requests, rather than expecting a perfect result from the first prompt.
Asking an AI to work through a problem step by step before giving its final answer, which often makes the reasoning more accurate.
When an AI agrees with you or flatters you instead of telling you the truth, especially if your question hints at the answer you want.
When an AI states something false, like a made-up fact or source, in a confident and believable way.
The original document or data behind a claim, such as a law, a study or an official page, instead of someone's summary of it.
A reference that says where a fact came from, such as a book, article or web link, so you can check it yourself.
Giving an AI real material to base its answer on, such as your own document or live search results, so it is less likely to invent things.
When an AI gives unfair or skewed results for some groups of people, usually because of patterns in the data it learned from.
A setup where a person reviews and approves what AI produces before it is used, instead of trusting it blindly.
Any detail that can point to a specific person, such as a full name, home address, phone number or ID number.
Private details that your employer or clients expect you to keep secret, such as unreleased plans, contracts or customer records.
How long a company keeps the data you give it, such as chat history, and whether it can use it later.
A setting that lets you say no to something, such as letting a company train its AI on your chats.
A set of rules from your employer or school that says what you may and may not do with certain tools, including AI.
The legal right of a creator to control who may copy, share or sell their work, which affects how you may reuse AI output.
Telling people when AI helped create your work, which some workplaces, schools and publishers require.
A fake video, image or audio clip made with AI that convincingly shows someone saying or doing something they never did.
Using AI to copy a real person's voice from a short recording, which scammers use to fake urgent calls from family.
A scam message that pretends to be from someone you trust to trick you into clicking a link or sharing private details.
A piece of your own writing that you paste into a prompt so the AI copies your voice and word choices.
A written, word-for-word record of a spoken meeting or call, which AI can turn into notes and summaries.
A comparison that explains something new by likening it to something you already know well.
Fixing messy data, such as duplicates, typos and inconsistent formats, so it is ready to be analysed.
Quickly producing many ideas without judging them first, so you can pick the best ones afterwards.
Someone who argues against an idea on purpose to expose weak points. You can ask an AI to play this role.
A reusable prompt with blanks that you fill in each time, saving you from rewriting the same instructions.
An AI helper built into an app you already use, such as email or documents, that can draft, summarize or answer questions.
An AI system that can plan and carry out several steps on its own, such as searching, writing and sending, to reach a goal.
The no-cost version of an online service, usually with limits on how much you can use it or which features you get.
An AI tool that creates pictures from a written description you give it.
A saved collection of your best prompts and templates, organised so you can reuse them quickly.
The set of steps you follow to get a task done, which can include AI at certain points along the way.
Short notes a company publishes about what changed in a new version of its product, useful for tracking AI tool updates.
